extraction.name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
extraction.description: A subset of 23 particularly challenging BIG-Bench tasks for which no prior result from Srivastava et al. (2022) has outperformed the average human-rater score. The dataset contains 6,511 evaluation examples in total.
extraction.creator: Mirac Suzgun, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, Jason Wei
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset is a curated subset of the BIG-Bench benchmark. It was created by filtering the original BIG-Bench tasks based on specific criteria: tasks with more than three subtasks were removed, tasks with fewer than 103 examples were removed, tasks without human-rater baselines were removed, and tasks that did not use multiple-choice or exact match evaluation metrics were removed. From the remaining clean tasks, those where the best reported model outperformed the average human-rater were excluded. Finally, 13 extremely difficult tasks requiring domain-specific knowledge or not practically solvable within twenty minutes were excluded, leaving 23 tasks.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The BIG-Bench benchmark (Srivastava et al., 2022), which consists of over 200 diverse text-based tasks.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors selected a subset of 23 tasks from BIG-Bench. For all but three tasks (Causal Judgement, Penguins in a Table, and Snarks), a random subset of 250 evaluation examples was taken. For the remaining three tasks, all available test examples were used (187, 146, and 178 respectively).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Filtering criteria included removing tasks with >3 subtasks, <103 examples, no human baselines, and non-multiple-choice/exact-match metrics. Tasks where prior models beat human raters were excluded. Tasks deemed too difficult or outside scope (e.g., requiring chess knowledge) were excluded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The original BIG-Bench tasks were annotated by a team of raters who manually solved each task and scored them against golden labels to establish human-rater baselines. For the BBH subset, the authors manually wrote three chain-of-thought (CoT) exemplars for each task to be used in prompting.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The human-rater scores are not representative of the entire population but express the empirical difficulty of a given task. The human-evaluation component took almost a year, during which task formatting and content changed multiple times. Human-raters could use external resources.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: A team of raters enlisted by the BIG-Bench organizers. No specific demographic details are provided.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The work aims to measure the capabilities and limitations of large language models. It discusses that surpassing average human-rater performance should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning. It also notes that some tasks require world knowledge or cultural context (e.g., Western society practices).
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The human-rater baselines may not be fully representative of human performance due to changes in task format/content during the year-long evaluation and the use of external resources. Some tasks rely on knowledge of Western society, humor, and names of artists/bands/movies in the West.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is a subset of 23 tasks. Some tasks were excluded because they were extremely difficult, required domain-specific knowledge, or were not practically solvable within twenty minutes. The human-rater baselines are not fully representative of the general population. The dataset does not include tasks that are outside the scope of the work (e.g., moral permissibility, checkmate in one).
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation of language model capabilities, specifically testing multi-step reasoning and the effectiveness of chain-of-thought prompting. It is used to benchmark models like PaLM, Codex, and InstructGPT.
